_comment: The routing table. Seeded once at install and never rewritten by an apply:
a file on the claw is somebody's ruling about this machine.
THIS FILE IS THE RECORD AND THE SERVICE SERVES IT. The service re-reads it
whenever the bytes change, so an edit made here reaches the running process
within one event and needs no restart. The `email` verbs write it back in
the key order this template carries, so a table the command has written and
this template differ only where a value differs.
self  is this claw's own identity on the wire. It is EMPTY on a fresh claw.
An operator fills it once, after the provider key is wired, with
`email inbox create --username <name> --display-name "<Name>"`.
The address is in every From: line a recipient ever sees, so a second
one is refused. There is no verb that changes it, and editing this
file is the deliberate way, which is a step somebody takes knowing
they have to tell everybody who holds the old address.
Nothing in a release carries a firm's address.
self.runbook is the absolute path of the firm's communication
runbook, the document the email orchestrator applies to everything
that goes out. It is EMPTY on a fresh claw. The launch that writes
the runbook records where it put it, with
`email self set runbook <path>`, and `email self clear runbook` puts
it back to empty. The command is the way to change this field. The
value is a pointer and nothing here opens it.
default   the handle every mail reaches when nothing else matches. This is
the email orchestrator, the agent that holds the judgement.
domains   sender domain to handles. This is where one mail fans out to
several desks.
addresses one address to handles, and `agent` marking an address as another
machine rather than a person. What that flag means for a reply is
the email orchestrator's runbook, not this service's code.
The thread map is NOT here. It lives beside this file in threads.jsonl and
the service owns it: a reply routes back to the desk that started the
conversation, whatever this table says about the sender.
